text:
I couldn't fail to notice another way to improve the efficiency of your setup: Just let it spin in the other direction!
As any winged aircraft, your drone suffers from  wing tip vortices due to induced drag. 
These vortices reduce the wing's ability to generate lift, so that it requires a higher angle of attack for the same lift, which tilts the total aerodynamic force rearwards and increases the drag component of that force.
In the flights you showed us, the propellers were turning in the same direction as the vortices, hence enhancing them. Now  if the drone spins in the other direction the wing tip vortices switch direction too. Since the spinning direction of the prop would stay the same, those vortices would be reduced by the prop spin.
The effect would be even more pronounced if the props would be at the very tip of the wing. 
See:
Chance Vought V-173
Chance Vought XF5U
Bell-Boeing V-22
On all these planes the outside tip of the props were moving downward.

text:
@NicholasRehm  The concept actually comes from a children's toy. It's a stick that you attach to a small propeller, and you rub it in your palms which causes it to spin, lift up and hover like a helicopter.

Putting that on a drone makes it more efficient, just like you touched on, the whole unit becomes one large, slow spinning, "passive" propeller.

Also, having tri-drone is a more efficient design than a quad-drone. You basically can have three larger active-propellers, rather than four smaller ones. So these two attributes fit together nicely.

The reason why people opt for the quad-drone setup is because it is actually more simple, cheaper, and easier to navigate (you can assign each side as front/back/left/right). Each of the four arms can be rigid and controlled by a simple on/off switch. A tri-drone needs more tweaks, and have each arm needing to pivot and spin at different rates.

As for energy source, fossil fuel is still better method at the medium to heavy weight. Electrical is only viable at the super lightweight scale. Not sure about nuclear, we don't have the technology for it (small nuclear engine). The best compromise is using solar energy for splitting water, generating hydrogen, using solar energy to compress it, then having hydrogen engine for helicopter flight. It can scale to heavyweight sizes, and is based on a renewable source.

@NicholasRehm    I've flown RC helis since the early 1990's, so a bit of experience on related things, so I'll just list out some ideas off hand..
1.  Get rid of the center part of the 'wings', and make the outer wing part bigger so it's more efficient.  Center part has a low speed, so it adds more weight while adding little lift.  Even with a lot of wash in toward the center, the center part still is usually terrible for weight to lift.  IOW from the length of the wings now, get rid of the inner 1/2, and make the remaining outer parts larger.  Might be more unstable like that though.  (If it's flying fast forward enough, the center 'whole disc' can give a lot of lift from translational lift.  But you can always add it back in later, and it adds more weight for hovering without much lift.)
2.  From 7:15 .   Realize this prop thrust idea is not the only thing going on.  In a plane, the thrust motor pulls the wing forward, and then a large lift force is generated by the wing at roughly 90 degrees to the thrust direction.  The force of lift is coming from tapping the generated pressure differential not the thrust motor directly.  Think of making the outboard wing sections large and glider wings, the diameter larger, and then having tiny motors that just pull the glider wings around for lift.  Should be able to beat your current 3:1 hover and make something that could approach a plane, you're largely operating as one if you make this big.  I'd be tempted to try and make a huge, light one just to see if you can catch thermals and fly it like a glider.
3.  Might be able to steer this with control surfaces on the outboard wings instead of directly by power.  Just something to check maybe, the motor thrust steering is probably fine, even if there was some 'gain' it would be pretty small.
4.  You can always reduce it to 1 rotary wing.  Look at the 1 rotor heli, and there are some one wing 'drones' similar to this idea with just one wing.  There are some modeled after the idea of a helicopter seed.  But I do prefer the 3

text: ​ @jeffl4802  Yes, it is pushing air down, just like a ceiling fan. Planes and helicopters obtain lift by equal-and-opposite-reaction: push against air; air pushes against you; if you're not secured, up you go. A positive angle of attack for a wing or horizontal rotor blade ensures that this effect is constant. Thus, even flat or symmetrically curved wings can provide lift. What you're talking about is the Bernoulli effect, which is real, and can also contribute to lift if the wing is curved (concave down), since the faster air over the top will be at a lower pressure than the slower air flowing under the bottom. But note that this does not "suck" the wing up; there is no such thing as suction. It just creates differential pressure that pushes the wing from the high-pressure area below to the low-pressure area above.

text: For every frame, make a triangle out of some easily identifiable feature (in your case maybe some differently colored retro reflectors placed on the ground, just to avoid any more complex image processing). Once you can identify the points of the triangle, calculate the center of the triangle. Compare one frame's triangle to the previous frame's and calculate how much rotation around the center minimizes the error of this frame to the last. That is the angle of rotation over the duration of the frame (1/60sec) for 60fps video). If you have known features, then you also have an absolute reference (ex: the blue reflector is north). Obviously a commercial solution would extract features from the environment, and thus have to determine ground truth in a different way, but for a test flight, this should give you angular velocity and orientation with very little computation.

text:
Hi Nicholas,
Airplane wings in normal level flight have a natural vortex at the tips where the difference in air pressure between the upper and lower surfaces generates the tip vortex through loss of underside pressure. That's why some airplanes have the folded up tip design, to try to cut the losses. Could you not use your engine rotation in the other direction to reverse the tip vortex losses and use the circular prop-wash to actually help charge each airfoil underside with higher pressure? 
Rather than moving your engine mountings to the tip of the airfoils,  just shorten your current airfoils to bring the tips to the engines, and then you could test the power efficiency. If you don't get any less lift for the same power with shorter wings then this should prove to be the efficiency savings at the tips votexes.
Most interesting videos, and some wonderful pieces of flying kit. Can't wait for the next installment on this one.
All the best :)

text:
A spinning drone will be practically useless, because the drone has a device called IMU to measure it's orientation. IMU is the hypothalamus of the drone. If you are planning to simply hover at one place, you don't need a drone for that. You can use the good old baloon.
Why the spinning drone gives more lift? Because by design, aircrafts are supposed to spend their thrust to counter drag, and gain lift.
For example, a biplane, spends it engine power to neutralize the drag of the propellor. The propellor gains lift in forward direction, and this lift neutralizes the drag experienced by it's wings. And wings finally lift the aircraft upward. So let's say, if you spend 1 N-m torque at the front propellor, you gain a lift of 5 N in forward direction. That 5 N forward pull, counters the 5 N drag of the wing. The wing returns 15 N upward lift. So By inversting 1 N-m torque, we are getting back 15 N upward lift.
You can create a 3 dimensional copter by neutralizing the drag at three levels. The lift of smaller propellor rotating in YZ plane, will neutralize the drag of medium size propellor rotating in XY plane. And the lift of medium size propellor(XY plane) will neutralize the drag of large size propellor rotating in ZX plane. So by investing small power in the YZ plane, you may get tremandous lift in the ZX plane. But at the end of the day such a drone will be useless, because IMU will not work in in it.
If we could do with rotating drones, we would catapult a boomerang in the sky. But most sensors will fail if the entire body rotates. We can still create hand grenades or relief packages, shaped like boomerang. Sensors are not necessary in every application - but such scenarios are rare.

You are actually not also inclusing the benefit of a couple of extra forces. If you can imagine that the propellar was facing horizontal at the end of the wing. You would lose some of your benefit. While the thrust created by the propellar would have less drag. Its vertical vector is zero, but its horizontal vector is 1. If we tilt it up by say 30 degrees, then the vertical vector is 0.5 and horizontal vector is 0.866. Typical stall angle of attack  for an aircraft is about 18 degrees. so more than 18 degrees not so optimal. But Even at 15 degrees you have a relative trust vertical vector of about 0.3
but you only lose a few percent of horizontal thrust. So if we keep the blade face perpendicular to the plane of the bottom of the wing, anywear from 13 to 17 degree wing angel of attack is beneficial. 
   The second thing here since is you have the propellar blowing over the wing, whereas you have the Angle of Attacked being realligned relative to the wing position, while it creates more turbulence on the outer wing, it creates a much higher lift on the wider part of the wing since the higher angles of attack given rise to 'stall' inefficiencies is partially being corrected by the action of the increase directed windflow behind the propellar. 
Ideally, one would want to see laminar flow from the prop to the wing, and I think the fluxes in lift created by the eddies from the propellar are causing the craft to pitch. One way to correct this is to finlets along the wing to keep the air from traveling radially down the wing. 
Some possibilites for improvement
1. Move the propellars closer in. 
2. Finlets behind the prop and at the end of the wing would help straighten out the airflow.

text:
Has no one here ever heard of a helicopter?
A large single rotor has always, and will always be more efficient at generating thrust than multiple smaller rotors.
Multirotor drones are a downgrade from helicopter designs in terms of efficiency, while being a more stable platform for shooting photos/videos.
Helicopter designs also rely more heavily on decent mechanical components for stability and control, as ideally you want to be able to adjust individual blade angle for yaw/pitch/roll control. Drones on the flip side can handle yaw/pitch/roll and stability control all through cheap electronics.

This design would be even more efficient if the large rotor was powered directly rather than three small rotors, with a tail rotor to counter the torque generated, though I guess that wouldn't make an interesting video.
